paper_title: N-Gram Memories at Two Bits: Quantizing Lookup Tables in Large Language Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Conditional memory expands language-model capacity through selective lookup, but the full embedding table must remain available for every possible input. We introduce Conditional Program (CP), a compressed representation that reconstructs only the rows an input requests. CP represents each row by a short code and a local scale, with a reconstruction program shared across the table. We instantiate this representation with a Gaussian trellis, norm restoration and independently decodable row records. CP's two-bit code lowers output KL by 41--63\% relative to 2-bit round-to-nearest. Analysis across three trained n-gram memory families shows that Gaussian-like coordinate statistics coexist with learned relationships among rows; at matched storage budgets, the shared trellis outperforms the fitted codebooks and low-rank residual variants we test. For DeepSeek, it reduces table storage from 203GB to 51GB, leaving room for larger workloads when the table is kept on GPU.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Conditional memory expands language-model capacity without proportional increase in per-token computation. It retrieves learned representations from large embedding tables, allowing model to use only small part of its memory for each input (Cheng et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026). This makes higher capacity attractive under limited compute budgets, but the tables still occupy substantial storage. Moving them from accelerator memory to host memory changes where that cost is paid without reducing it. Compressing conditional memory presents different challenge from conventional LLM weight compression. Although its embedding tables contain learned parameters, they are accessed through sparse, input-dependent lookups rather than dense computation. Existing LLM compression methods primarily target dense model weights, leaving 1 the distinct access patterns of conditional memory largely unaddressed. Conditional memory instead requires reducing the footprint of the entire table while preserving independent access to individual rows and the information they provide to the model. Can conditional memory be stored more compactly while reconstructing only the entries needed by the current input? We propose Conditional Program (CP), representation that stores instructions for reconstructing each entry through shared decoder. Our hypothesis is that compact shared reconstruction rule, together with short row-specific codes and local scales, can preserve the signal that the model consumes from the table. An input selects which entries to reconstruct, so the extra work is confined to the rows it accesses. This exchanges storage across the full table for reconstruction work on small subset, carrying the selective use of conditional memory into its compressed representation. Specifically, CP represents each row with short code and local scale, using decoder shared across the table. We model normalized row contents as the accumulation of many small learning contributions dispersed across coordinates; when these contributions are weakly dependent and none dominates, Gaussian source approximation follows from central-limit argument. Therefore, we encode rows in their stored coordinate system with shared Gaussian trellis (Tseng et al., 2024b). The local scale restores the decoded vectors norm, and independently stored row records allow the runtime to fetch and reconstruct only requested entries (Figure 1). At two bits, CP reduces table storage by roughly fourto eightfold, with most reported task scores remaining close to their original values. For 4,096-token DeepSeek prefill from host memory, its row layout reduces lookup time from 10.78 to 6.54 ms compared with QTIP tile-window decoder in layout microbenchmark. We introduce Conditional Program, representation that exchanges storage across the full memory table for reconstruction work on the few entries selected by each input. We instantiate CP with shared Gaussian trellis, per-row norm restoration and independently addressable records, preserving selective access in the compressed representation. We evaluate downstream performance across diverse tasks, analyze compression fidelity, and measure lookup costs and workload capacity under GPU and host-memory placement.

sections.title: 3.2 Gaussian Source Modeling
sections.content: Conditional-memory embeddings are learned through repeated updates from diverse inputs and contexts. In hashed n-gram memories, for example, multiple n-grams may map to the same row, allowing different training signals to contribute to shared representation (Cheng et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026). When such contributions are distributed across many coordinates, an approximately isotropic direction provides useful intuition for the resulting representation. In high dimensions, isotropically distributed directions exhibit approximately Gaussian coordinate statistics after normalization (Diaconis and Freedman, 1987). Motivated by this intuition, we model the normalized row contents using common Gaussian source while keeping row magnitudes separate. Specifically, we approximate the coordinate distribution of zi by standard Gaussian distribution (0, 1). This source model provides common statistical basis for representing different rows through shared reconstruction rule, while row-specific codes capture their individual contents.

sections.title: 3.3 Encoding and Norm Restoration
sections.content: To encode the Gaussian source, we instantiate the shared reconstruction rule using trellis-coded quantization (TCQ) (Marcellin and Fischer, 1990; Mao and Gray, 2010). TCQ represents sequence of values through path of state transitions, allowing reconstruction values to be selected jointly rather than quantizing each coordinate independently. We use Gaussian HYB bitshift trellis with tail-biting. For each row, the encoder searches for low-error path through the shared trellis and stores its transition symbols as ci. The reconstruction function recovers the corresponding vector from these symbols using small shared lookup table and arithmetic operations. All rows use the same coding rule and code rate, without an additional coordinate rotation. Although the shared source model describes normalized row contents, the magnitude of each embedding also affects the signal passed to the model. least-squares reconstruction scale can shrink the decoded vector when its direction differs from the original row. CP instead restores the original row norm by setting αi = ei2/f (ci)2. This preserves the magnitude of the learned representation, even when doing so increases coordinate reconstruction error. The scale is computed once during encoding and stored with the corresponding row. 3.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: We evaluate how well CP preserves model quality under reduced table storage. We first compare downstream task performance at low bit rates, then examine the trade-off between storage and outputdistribution fidelity across wider range of rates.

sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Models. We evaluate Conditional Program (CP) on three models that employ n-gram lookup tables: DeepSeek, Qwen, and LongCat, as described in Section 2.1. To isolate the effect of compression, we compress only the lookup tables while keeping all other model components unchanged. Benchmarks. To assess the impact of compression across different model capabilities, we evaluate 40 tasks spanning five categories: commonsense, knowledge, reading comprehension, multilingual understanding, and math and code. Beyond knowledge-intensive benchmarks, we include GSM8K and HumanEval to evaluate mathematical reasoning and code generation, both of which require generated answers. Table 1 presents seven representative benchmark columns from this suite. Baselines. We first compare against the original lookup tables and table removal, where every lookup returns zero, to assess the contribution of the stored entries. For quantization baselines, we include round-to-nearest (RTN), which independently rounds values to the nearest quantization level, and NVFP4 and MXFP4, which use four-bit floating-point formats (Rouhani et al., 2023). To further examine the benefits of CPs design, we adapt the trellis quantization of QTIP (Tseng et al., 2024b), originally developed for dense weights, to lookup tables. Specifically, we construct trellisbased baseline with within-row rotation and global scale shared across the table, allowing us to distinguish the benefits of trellis quantization from those of CPs row-wise magnitude separation.

sections.title: 5.1 Selective Lookup
sections.content: pendix G.1. Lookup layouts. CP stores each row as an independent record, allowing only the requested rows to be fetched and reconstructed. In contrast, QTIPs tiled representation distributes each row across multiple code fragments. To enable selective access with this layout, we implement tile-window decoder that retrieves only the bit windows needed for the requested rows rather than entire tiles. We compare this decoder against our fused row-wise decoder under identical lookup requests, two-bit code rate, and per-row scale storage. The tiled baseline uses random payloads, while CP uses encoded model tables, so this experiment isolates access cost rather than reconstruction fidelity. Lookup latency. We replay lookup requests from 4,096-token sequences constructed from held-out FineWeb-Edu text using the DeepSeek tokenizer on single H200 GPU. Each token requests 48 rows across two Engram layers. With tables stored in GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM), CP completes the requests in 0.190 ms, compared with 0.221 ms for the tile-window decoder. When accessing pinned host DRAM over PCIe, the corresponding times are 6.54 ms and 10.78 ms. These results demonstrate that CPs row-wise representation supports efficient selective lookup, with particularly large benefits when accessing tables across PCIe. We report the mean of five independent run medians, each measured over 100 timed calls after 20 warm-up calls. Additional comparisons and memory-access analyses are provided in Ap-

sections.title: 5.2 Workload Capacity
sections.content: Experimental setup. To evaluate the serving benefits of reduced memory usage, we distribute the DeepSeek backbone and tables across four or eight H200 GPUs. Our representative workload processes eight sequences with 4,096-token prompts and generates 256 tokens per sequence. We additionally evaluate larger workloads, including decode batch of 512 sequences and prefill step of 65,536 tokens across 32 sequences. Table 5 summarizes the results. Four-GPU serving. With four GPUs, the original FP8 tables occupy 50.7 GB per GPU, compared with 12.7 GB for CP. For the representative workload, CP reduces prefill latency from 64.66 to 13.27 and enables larger workloads that otherwise run out of memory. Compared with the four-bit NVFP4 baseline, CP also reduces the 64k-token prefill time from 59.81 to 18.23 s, while decode times remain similar. These results show that CP alleviates GPU memory pressure and improves performance for memory-intensive serving workloads. Eight-GPU serving. With eight GPUs, the original FP8 tables fit comfortably for smaller workloads, and step times differ by at most 2.4% when memory pressure is limited. However, CP frees an additional 19.0 GB per GPU, allowing substantially larger workloads. On the tested grid, the largest successful decode batch increases from 1,024 to at least 2,048 sequences, while prefill capacity in7 creases from 96k to at least 128k tokens. These results demonstrate that CPs reduced memory footprint translates into greater serving capacity, even when smaller workloads already fit in GPU memory. Detailed workload configurations and measurements are provided in Appendix G. Together, these results highlight two complementary benefits of CP for model serving. Its row-wise representation enables efficient selective lookup, while its compact storage reduces GPU memory pressure, improving serving performance and supporting larger workloads.

sections.title: 6 Related Work
sections.content: LLM weight quantization. GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2023) and AWQ (Lin et al., 2024) use calibration activations to guide rounding or scaling, while QuIP, QuIP#, QuaRot and SpinQuant use coordinate transformations to make weights easier to quantize (Chee et al., 2023; Tseng et al., 2024a; Ashkboos et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025). AQLM learns additive codebooks (Egiazarian et al., 2024); QTIP combines incoherence processing with trellis coding (Tseng et al., 2024b), and HIGGS uses Gaussian-optimal grids (Malinovskii et al., 2025). CP applies Gaussian trellis coding to frozen lookup rows without rotation, restoring each rows norm and storing it independently for selective access. Because quantization can affect factual answers even when perplexity changes little (Jaiswal et al., 2024; Namburi et al., 2023; Dutta et al., 2024), we evaluate absolute task scores alongside output KL. Embedding-table compression. Row-wise lowbit quantization is established for recommender embeddings (Guan et al., 2019; Khudia et al., 2021); other approaches use low-precision training, frequency-based mixed precision, or structures fixed during training (Yang et al., 2020; Li et al., 2023, 2024; Shi et al., 2020; Yin et al., 2021; Desai et al., 2022; Tsang and Ahle, 2023). For LLM input embeddings, CARVQ combines grouped residual VQ with corrective MLP trained for each model (Gou et al., 2025). The hashed tables studied here share rows among colliding n-grams. CP compresses these already trained tables using their row values, with shared decoder, no model retraining and no frequency-based bit allocation. Conditional-memory structure and placement. TN-gram replaces hashed tables with tensor decomposition during pretraining (Zhou et al., 2026); TF-Engram and CXL-based systems address memory placement and access (Ma et al., 2026b,a). TF-Engrams hash-based compression shares slots between n-grams, whereas CP numerically compresses the rows of an existing table. SCONE stores n-gram embeddings computed by separate model off the accelerator (Yu et al., 2025). Product-key memories and memory layers retrieve rows through learned key search (Lample et al., 2019; Berges et al., 2024); the tables studied here use hashes of input tokens.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: CP compresses lookup tables with row codes, local scales and shared decoder while preserving independent access to requested rows. Across three hashed-memory models, two-bit codes reduce table storage by roughly fourto eightfold, with most reported task scores close to their original values despite some taskand model-dependent losses. Under GPU memory pressure, smaller tables allow larger workloads and reduce prefill time. When memory is sufficient, complete inference steps show little speed improvement in our implementation.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: concern Coverage. Our postconclusions training compression of three models with hashed lookup tables; they need not extend to other memory architectures, including token-indexed tables (Appendix H). Most downstream comparisons use the two primary code rates, with less task coverage at higher rates than in the KL sweep. Small task-score differences do not establish equivalence. Analysis. The fitted-codebook and structuredresidual comparisons evaluate output KL only on Qwen, limiting their generality across models. Some equal-budget comparisons use interpolated trellis values without uncertainty estimates. The Gaussian source approximation does not establish how training produces the observed row statistics. Deployment. Serving measurements use single node and eager inference; optimized engines may spend different fraction of time on lookup. Some configurations have only one measurement run, and tested workload limits are not exact capacity thresholds. Access counts come from English web text, so frequency-based allocation and caching results may change with the deployment distribution.

The 40 tasks form five reporting groups: commonsense (7), knowledge (7), reading comprehension (2), multilingual (22), and math and code (2). The last group contains GSM8K and HumanEval. MGSM remains in the multilingual group, where its six languages are scored separately. A.2 Output fidelity and statistics Each domain is tokenized with the models own tokenizer and cut into 2,047-token chunks: 128 per domain for web, code, math, chat and multi5 (262,016 tokens), and 16 per language for the 15 languages of multi15 (491,280 tokens), 880 chunks per setting. Documents are normally truncated to 4,000 characters, and those under 200 characters are dropped; short multi15 language sets fall back to untruncated documents. Statistics. All intervals are 95% percentile bootstrap intervals with seed 0. Task scores and benefit retained use 2,000 item-bootstrap replicates; KL uses 2,000 replicates over 2,047-token chunks, paired across settings for ratios; paired task differences use 10,000 item replicates. The trellis uses 16-bit state, two values per step and tail-biting with two Viterbi passes. Its HYB table is built from 512-entry k-means codebook of 2-D standard Gaussian. The code scale factor is .95 at 23 bits, .90 at 3.5 bits and .85 at 4 bits on DeepSeek and Qwen; LongCat uses 1.0 at 2 bits and the same values above; at 1.5 bits the factors are 1.0 and 1.05. The rate is + 16/d bpp; the shared lookup table is not counted for DeepSeek and Qwen and adds about 6 106 bpp for LongCat. RTN stores minimum and scale per group, counted as 2 16 bits. NVFP4 has an e4m3 scale per 16 values and one fp32 scale per table (4.5 bpp); MXFP4 has power-of-two scale per 32 values (4.25 bpp). Encoding cost and software. Encoding the 2bit CP table takes about 3.1 on 4 H200 GPUs for DeepSeek (about 12 GPU-hours), 0.83 on 4 GPUs for Qwen, and 5.18 summed over LongCats 12 tables. Software is PyTorch 2.14.0 and Transformers 5.17.0. The k-means table is not bitreproducible across independent encodes, so the LS controls reuse the stored symbols of the normrestoration tables. The Qwen RTN baseline keeps its scale and minimum in fp32 although its rate counts them as bf16. The table sizes in the main results are logical code and metadata sizes. sections.content: End-to-end serving runs and the unfused lookup controls use one node with 8 H200 GPUs, two Xeon Platinum 8462Y+ CPUs, 2 TB of DRAM and 6 local PM1733a NVMe drives in RAID-0. Peak GPU memory in Section 5 and Table 23 is PyTorchs max_memory_allocated in units of 109 bytes, taken on the GPU with the largest value. It counts allocated tensors only, not memory the allocator has reserved but not handed out. G.1 Records and lookup kernels Each CP row is fixed-size record. The record holds the trellis bitstream of the row and one bf16 scale αi (Section 3). b-bit code on d-value row takes bd/8 bytes, and the scale adds 2 bytes. The rate is therefore + 16/d bpp. For DeepSeek at = 2 and = 256, record is 64 + 2 = 66 B, or 2.06 bpp. For Qwen at = 160, it is 40 + 2 = 42 B, or 2.10 bpp. On SSD the records are aligned so that no record crosses 4 KB page, and one row is one read. Table 24 compares lookup layouts on DeepSeek. The fused comparison uses one H200 on fourGPU node with Xeon Platinum 8462Y+ CPUs, PyTorch 2.14.1+cu130 and Triton 3.8.0. CPU execution and host allocations are bound to NUMA node 0; GPU clocks are not locked. The full 768,022,850row tables use real CP codes and random tile payloads, with the same real row scales and decoder lookup table. G.3 Caching and host placement In the DeepSeek host-memory tests, compressing the table from 202.7 to 50.7 GB saves capacity and speeds up isolated lookups. Lookup accounts for less than 1% of forward step in our eager implementation without graph capture, so complete step time changes little; the backbone remains on the GPU. Figure 4 comes from simulation of static hot-row cache. The cache holds the rows with the highest FineWeb-Edu read counts (Appendix D.1), and we evaluate it on held-out FineWeb-Edu reads. Each missed row costs one 4 KB read. The simulation uses the fio constants above, 2.56M IOPS and 91 µs at queue depth 1.
